fields.AN_Notes: Systematic review of machine learning risk models in child welfare. Bias axes follow the review's own coding scheme of racial and socioeconomic equity. Harm types follow the review's own coding dimensions: data-source limitations (racial disparities in data, proxy variables, oversurveillance) as indirect discrimination in risk scores, and the equity evaluation category of comparing AUC across racial groups as disparate performance. Mitigation inventory synthesised from the reviewed studies: exclusion of race variables and protective-factor predictors (Pre_Processing), separate models for Maori children (In_Training), equity consultant, withholding scores from investigators, participatory design and a proposed uniform reporting protocol (Organisational_Process). Evaluated refers to a synthesised evaluation, not the review's own experiment: the separate-model approach of Wilson et al. (2015) was assessed and did not achieve the desired effect; the other measures stay at proposed or demonstrated level. Bias is defined by the review as caseworker beliefs influencing decisions, next to separate definitions of ethics and equity. Asset-based and strengths-based approaches are practice orientations, not a theory framing bias.

fields.AN_Notes: Interview study with a ChatGPT prompt case study. Prompts (story prompts with person replaced by man, woman, non-binary person) serve as research instrument and as a proposed bias test suite; no named prompting technique. Bias axes: gender with cisgender men, cisgender women and non-binary or transgender participants; the non-binary and transgender comparison is coded additionally as Sexual_Orientation_Identity because it concerns gender identity. Harm types from the work's own output analysis and interview results: stereotyped role attributions, cis-centric default and gender assignment to neutral characters, reduction of non-binary characters to identity struggles. Accuracy was perceived as similar across groups, so no Disparate_Performance; tone differences are not coded. Mitigation proposals only: diversified training data and data curation (Pre_Processing), clarifying questions when prompts are vague (Intra_Processing), gender-inclusive co-design, real-time and community bias auditing (Organisational_Process). Bias is not defined; the understanding follows from stereotype and representation framing. Grounded theory and reflexive thematic analysis are methods, not a theory framing gender or bias.

fields.AN_Notes: Social opinion mining of 2022 tweets on AI and gender by female users. Bias axes: gender as object and race through hypothesis H4 and the chi-square test of gender and race co-occurrence in tweets. Intersectional is not coded because the analysis measures co-occurrence of topics in tweets, not an outcome that depends on the combination; the matrix-of-domination interpretation stays in the theory reference. Harm types None: the harm mechanisms (stereotyped assistants, biased facial recognition, recruitment inequities, male-dominated development) are cited from other work and the own results concern discourse and user behaviour. Mitigation proposals are organisational: multidisciplinary teams, legal frameworks, parity in development teams, support for women in STEM and women-led AI ventures. Gender understanding follows the analysis, which classifies users binarily with a name dictionary and she/her or he/him keywords; the introduction mentions gender as a narrow social construct without the analysis following it. AN_Task None: NLP is the authors' research method, not a task of professional practice; the closing sentence proposes opinion mining for decision-makers outside social work.

fields.AN_Notes: Critical review of 30 AI fairness papers against Collins and Bilge's six intersectionality tenets. Bias axes: gender and race with Black women as the worked example of intersectional subgroups that the review's own argument uses; the argument that subgroup fairness misses interlocking oppression depends on the combination. Harm types from the review's own findings about AI fairness research: people at the margins erased by purely technical fairness practice (Erasure) and Western contexts as unexamined default (Exclusionary_Norms); allocational and representational harms are mentioned only in general. Mitigation stages: the review structures its synthesis by the pipeline stage at which reviewed papers operationalise intersectionality (pre-, in-, post-processing) and gives organisational recommendations (reflexivity, citational integrity, community engagement, leadership incentives); no synthesised evaluation with a reported result, so Proposed. Gender definition coded Explicit through the adopted Collins and Bilge determination that power produces social divisions including gender; this also carries Social_Construct.

fields.AN_Notes: Philosophical argument that AI bias is structural injustice (Young), with health-care AI as case study along four development stages. Bias axes are the worked examples of the own stage analysis: race (skin-cancer data, cost proxy, VBAC scores), gender (gender research gap, menstruation tracking) and class or income (10/90 funding gap, EHR availability, insurance). Harm types are those the own stage analysis and recognition argument establish with worked examples: better performance for light-skinned patients (Disparate_Performance), race as explicit VBAC input (Direct_Discrimination), health-care cost and ZIP code as proxies (Indirect_Discrimination), menstruation tracking omitted (Erasure), degrading stereotypes of Black women in search (Stereotyping). Mitigation: own recommendations in Table 1 are Proposed (representative datasets and reference-standard review as Pre_Processing; diverse stakeholder engagement, deliberative minipublics, resource distribution, deployment checks and monitoring as Organisational_Process). Evaluated refers only to the synthesised case of Pierson et al. (2021), whose patient-reported labels and diverse dataset reduced unexplained pain disparities; it is not the paper's own experiment. AN_Task Other_Task: clinical diagnosis and health-needs assessment, outside social work. Gender is treated as an axis of structural inequality without a determination or a recognisable understanding, so Absent and Unclear.

fields.AN_Notes: Case study of the grassroots organisation Queer in AI with community and aid-recipient survey data. The AI harms in section 2 are cited from other work; the own analysis concerns exclusion of queer people from AI research, conferences and publishing. Bias axes are those the own analysis develops for barriers to participation: sexual orientation and gender identity, gender (trans and non-binary scholars, deadnaming), income (application fees, low-income scholars), Global South and visa processes (Nationality_Migration), disability and neurodivergence, and the compounding of intersecting identities; ethnicity appears only in survey demographics and is not coded. Harm types from the organisers' own documentation: exclusionary gender collection and legal-name requirements on conference platforms (Exclusionary_Norms) and chat software blocking queer terms, deadnaming in proceedings (Erasure). Mitigation is organisational and community-led (decentralised participation, inclusive conference guide, name-change advocacy, citation-check tool, aid program); the initiatives are applied with survey feedback and adoption reports but without a completed assessment of a bias mitigation, so Demonstrated. Gender is not defined; survey categories include non-binary, genderqueer and further genders. Bias is not defined and is understood through discrimination and harm framing.
